questions.question: What is a product roadmap and what should it include?
questions.model_answer: A product roadmap is a strategic document that communicates the vision, direction, priorities, and progress of a product over time. It should include: product vision/goals (the 'why'), time horizons (now/next/later or quarterly themes), major initiatives or epics, key milestones and launches, dependencies, and success metrics for each initiative. Good roadmaps are outcomes-based (focused on customer problems and business results) rather than feature-based (a list of things to build).
questions.tip: Distinguish between an outcome roadmap (preferred) and a feature roadmap. Interviewers at modern product companies will push back on pure feature lists.

questions.question: How would you prioritise a backlog with limited engineering resources?
questions.model_answer: Use a prioritisation framework. RICE: Score = (Reach × Impact × Confidence) / Effort. ICE: Impact, Confidence, Ease. MoSCoW: Must have, Should have, Could have, Won't have. Start by aligning items to strategic goals, then score them. Always consider: (1) customer impact (pain severity × frequency), (2) business value (revenue, retention), (3) effort and risk, (4) dependencies. Hold a prioritisation session with engineering and design to validate effort estimates. Revisit the backlog at least monthly.
questions.tip: Show you can handle stakeholder pressure: 'I use data plus structured frameworks so prioritisation decisions are defensible, not political.'

questions.question: What is the difference between a user story and an epic?
questions.model_answer: An epic is a large body of work that can be broken down into smaller pieces; it represents a significant feature or goal (e.g. 'User Authentication System'). A user story is a small, specific piece of work described from the user's perspective: 'As a [user], I want to [action] so that [benefit].' Stories should be INVEST: Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable. An epic typically contains multiple user stories; a sprint delivers several stories contributing to an epic.
questions.tip: Write a sample user story live if asked: it shows you genuinely understand the format.

questions.question: How do you define and measure product-market fit?
questions.model_answer: Product-market fit (PMF) means the product satisfies a strong market demand. Key indicators: (1) Sean Ellis 'how disappointed' survey — if >40% of active users say they'd be 'very disappointed' if the product disappeared, you likely have PMF; (2) Retention curves that flatten rather than continuing to decline (a flat retention curve means some users find the product indispensable); (3) Organic growth / NPS > 50; (4) Revenue retention (net revenue retention > 100% for SaaS). PMF is not binary — it's a direction, and you reach it segment by segment.
questions.tip: Mention that you can have PMF in a niche before expanding. Over-expansion before PMF is a common startup killer.

questions.question: Walk me through how you would conduct a competitive analysis.
questions.model_answer: Steps: (1) Identify competitors — direct (same solution, same problem), indirect (different solution, same problem), and substitutes. (2) Define evaluation criteria aligned to your customers' decision factors: pricing, features, UX, integrations, support, performance. (3) Gather data: product trial, public reviews (G2, Capterra), analyst reports, job postings (job ads reveal what they're building), sales win/loss data. (4) Organise findings in a comparison matrix. (5) Identify whitespace — gaps competitors don't address that your users need. (6) Update quarterly; competitive landscape shifts.
questions.tip: Always connect competitive analysis to a product decision. Raw data without 'so what' is not analysis.

questions.question: How would you approach building a 0-to-1 product versus improving an existing product?
questions.model_answer: 0-to-1 (new product): focus on deep customer discovery (jobs-to-be-done interviews), build a tight feedback loop with early adopters, minimise scope to the core value proposition, treat everything as an experiment, and define a clear beachhead market. Metrics: engagement, retention, and qualitative signal over revenue. Improving existing product: you have data — use funnels, cohorts, and A/B testing to identify friction and opportunity; changes must not break existing user mental models; consider technical debt; success metrics are more quantitative (conversion, NPS delta, revenue impact). The key difference: 0-to-1 requires more qualitative discovery; 1-N requires more quantitative optimisation.
questions.tip: Interviewers love this question because it separates generalists from those who've actually done both. Be honest about which you've done.

questions.question: What metrics would you track for a SaaS subscription product and why?
questions.model_answer: Core SaaS metrics: (1) MRR/ARR — monthly/annual recurring revenue, the health metric. (2) Churn rate — monthly subscriber loss; <2% monthly is healthy for SMB. (3) Net Revenue Retention (NRR) — expansion minus churn; >100% means growth from existing customers alone. (4) CAC (Customer Acquisition Cost) vs LTV (Lifetime Value) — LTV:CAC > 3 is a benchmark for a healthy unit economics model. (5) Time to Value (TTV) — how quickly users reach the 'aha moment'. (6) DAU/MAU — engagement ratio. (7) NPS — leading indicator of retention. Prioritise NRR and TTV as the most actionable.
questions.tip: Show you can connect a metric to a concrete decision: 'If TTV is high, I'd invest in onboarding improvement, not acquisition.'

questions.question: Tell me about a time you had to gather requirements from multiple stakeholders with conflicting priorities.
questions.model_answer: STAR: Situation — for a university project, marketing wanted a flashy landing page with animations; the accessibility team insisted on a screen-reader-friendly, minimalist design. Task — I needed to align both groups into a single specification. Action — I ran individual stakeholder interviews to understand the underlying needs (marketing: conversion; accessibility: compliance and inclusivity). I reframed the discussion around shared goals and proposed a design with high-contrast, readable typography that still had a distinctive visual style. I facilitated one joint session to review the prototype. Result — both teams approved the design; the page met WCAG 2.1 AA and achieved a 12% higher click-through rate than the previous version.
questions.tip: Show you uncovered root needs, not just surface requests. That's the PM superpower.

questions.question: Describe a product decision you made that turned out to be wrong. What did you learn?
questions.model_answer: STAR: Situation — I pushed to add advanced filter functionality to our search feature, convinced it was a top user need. Task — I led the prioritisation and spec. Action — we shipped after 3 sprints. Result — adoption was 4% and support tickets didn't drop. Post-mortem: I had relied on vocal power users in our Slack community who were atypical. I hadn't looked at usage data first — 80% of searches were simple keyword queries. Learning: always triangulate qualitative user feedback with quantitative usage data before committing engineering resources.
questions.tip: Showing you can admit a mistake and articulate a changed behaviour is more impressive than a perfect story.

questions.question: Tell me about a time you led a cross-functional team through a high-stakes launch.
questions.model_answer: STAR: Situation — we were launching a payments feature in three new countries with a hard regulatory deadline. Task — I was the PM coordinating legal, engineering, compliance, localisation, and marketing across 4 time zones. Action — I created a shared launch tracker with weekly checkpoints, ran daily standups in the final 2 weeks, managed a risk register with owners for each blocker, and escalated one legal dependency to VP level 3 weeks before launch. Result — we launched in all three countries on the compliance deadline with zero P0 bugs and 98% uptime in the first week.
questions.tip: Emphasise your process for managing risk and escalation. Senior PMs are measured on predictability, not just outcomes.

questions.question: What is a North Star Metric and how do you choose one?
questions.model_answer: A North Star Metric (NSM) is the single metric that best captures the core value your product delivers to customers and that predicts long-term business success. Criteria for a good NSM: (1) reflects customer value (not a vanity metric like page views); (2) is measurable and unambiguous; (3) leads revenue, not lags it; (4) the whole team can influence it. Examples: Airbnb — nights booked; Spotify — time spent listening; Slack — messages sent per active user. Choose by asking: 'What is the one number that, if it grows, confirms our customers are getting value?'
questions.tip: Contrast NSM with vanity metrics (downloads, page views). Interviewers test whether you know the difference.

questions.question: Describe the process of running a successful sprint review.
questions.model_answer: A sprint review is a Scrum ceremony at the end of each sprint where the team demonstrates completed work to stakeholders. Steps: (1) Invite stakeholders (not just the team); (2) Demo working software — not slides; (3) Review which sprint goal items are Done vs incomplete; (4) Gather stakeholder feedback to inform the next sprint; (5) Update the backlog based on feedback; (6) Discuss any changes in market or priority. Keep it ≤4 hours for a 2-week sprint. The outcome is an updated backlog and shared understanding of product direction.
questions.tip: Emphasise 'working software' over reports. Stakeholders engaging with real features give better feedback.

questions.question: Why do you want to become a Product Manager?
questions.model_answer: I'm drawn to product management because it sits at the intersection of customer empathy, business strategy, and technical execution — three areas I'm passionate about. I've always been someone who asks 'why does this exist?' and 'how could this be better?' My background in [relevant experience] gave me exposure to customer problems and I found myself naturally thinking about solutions at the product level, not just my individual contribution. I want to shape the direction of products that genuinely improve people's lives, and PM is the role where I can do that most directly.
questions.tip: Make it personal — connect to a specific product experience that sparked your interest. Generic answers don't land.
